section.title: The Nazirite Vow
section.sectionRationale: Between the case laws of chapter 5 and the leaders' offerings of chapter 7 sits one of the most personal passages in Numbers: the voluntary vow of the Nazirite, by which any Israelite, man or woman, could set themselves apart to the LORD for a season, followed immediately by the priestly blessing that closes the whole Sinai legislation with grace rather than law.
section.thesis: Ordinary Israelites could voluntarily consecrate themselves to the LORD through the Nazirite vow, abstaining from the vine, from cutting their hair, and from contact with the dead, and this whole unit culminates in Aaron's blessing, God's own gracious words placed on His people's lives, showing that consecration finds its true rest not in vows kept but in the blessing God freely gives.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the voluntary vow of separation and its restrictions; the provision for accidental defilement during the vow; the offerings and rites that complete the vow; and the Aaronic blessing that closes the section.

units.label: The vow of separation
units.note: abstaining from the vine, from cutting hair, and from the dead

verses.text: And the LORD said to Moses,
“Speak to the Israelites and tell them that if a man or woman makes a special vow, the vow of a {{nazir|Nazirite}}, to separate himself to the LORD,
he is to abstain from wine and strong drink. He must not drink vinegar made from wine or strong drink, and he must not drink any grape juice or eat fresh grapes or raisins.
All the days of his separation, he is not to eat anything that comes from the grapevine, not even the seeds or skins.

For the entire period of his vow of separation, no razor shall pass over his head. He must be holy until the time of his separation to the LORD is complete; he must let the hair of his head grow long.
Throughout the days of his separation to the LORD, he must not go near a dead body.
Even if his father or mother or brother or sister should die, he is not to defile himself, because the crown of consecration to his God is upon his head.
Throughout the time of his separation, he is holy to the LORD.
If someone suddenly dies in his presence and defiles his consecrated head of hair, he must shave his head on the day of his cleansing, the seventh day.
On the eighth day he must bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.

And the priest is to offer one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering to make atonement for him, because he has sinned by being in the presence of the dead body. On that day he must consecrate his head again.
He must rededicate his time of separation to the LORD and bring a year-old male lamb as a guilt offering. But the preceding days shall not be counted, because his separation was defiled.
Now this is the law of the Nazirite when his time of separation is complete: He must be brought to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting,

and he is to present an offering to the LORD of an unblemished year-old male lamb as a burnt offering, an unblemished year-old female lamb as a sin offering, and an unblemished ram as a peace offering,
together with their grain offerings and drink offerings, and a basket of unleavened cakes made from fine flour mixed with oil and unleavened wafers coated with oil.
The priest is to present all these before the LORD and make the sin offering and the burnt offering.
He shall also offer the ram as a peace offering to the LORD, along with the basket of unleavened bread. And the priest is to offer the accompanying grain offering and drink offering.
Then at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, the Nazirite is to shave his consecrated head, take the hair, and put it on the fire under the peace offering.

And the priest is to take the boiled shoulder from the ram, one unleavened cake from the basket, and one unleavened wafer, and put them into the hands of the Nazirite who has just shaved the hair of his consecration.

The priest shall then wave them as a wave offering before the LORD. This is a holy portion for the priest, in addition to the breast of the wave offering and the thigh that was presented. After that, the Nazirite may drink wine.

This is the law of the Nazirite who vows his offering to the LORD for his separation, in addition to whatever else he can afford; he must fulfill whatever vow he makes, according to the law of his separation.”
Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Tell Aaron and his sons: This is how you are to {{bless|bless}} the Israelites. Say to them:
‘May the LORD bless you and keep you;
may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you;
may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace.’
So they shall put My name on the Israelites, and I will bless them.”

nazir.gloss: One separated or consecrated. From a root meaning to separate, nazir describes someone who has voluntarily set themselves apart to the LORD for a period, marked visibly by uncut hair, abstinence from the vine, and avoidance of the dead.

bless.gloss: To bless, to speak good and favor over someone. Used three times in the rising rhythm of the Aaronic blessing, barak here is not a wish but a divinely commanded pronouncement through which God Himself blesses His people, verse 27.

basic.context: Chapter 6 gives instructions for the Nazirite vow, a voluntary act of consecration open to any Israelite, man or woman, who wished to set themselves apart to the LORD for a period by abstaining from wine, from cutting their hair, and from contact with the dead. The chapter closes with the famous priestly blessing Aaron and his sons were to speak over Israel.
basic.hermeneutics: The Nazirite vow was a real, voluntary practice available to ordinary people, not a status reserved for priests or a mere symbol. The blessing that follows is not a magic formula but words God commands His priests to speak, promising that He Himself will bless and keep His people; both halves of the chapter show holiness and grace held together, consecration and benediction.
basic.originalLanguages: The word nazir comes from a root meaning to separate or consecrate, describing someone set apart to the LORD for a time by a voluntary vow. The blessing itself turns on barak, to bless, spoken three times in a rising rhythm of blessing, grace, and peace that has shaped Jewish and Christian worship for millennia.
basic.typology: The Nazirite's total consecration, especially the uncut hair as a visible sign of devotion, anticipates the entire, unbroken consecration of Christ; more directly, the priestly blessing itself anticipates the greater blessing God gives His people in Christ, in whom every spiritual blessing is found, Ephesians 1:3.
basic.christ: The Aaronic blessing asks that God's face shine upon His people and grant them peace, a request answered fully in Jesus Christ, in whom God's face is truly seen, 2 Corinthians 4:6, and through whom lasting peace with God is made, Romans 5:1. Christ is greater than any Nazirite, wholly consecrated to God, and He is the one through whom the blessing spoken here becomes final and unbreakable.
basic.god: God delights to bless His people; the blessing is not something Israel must extract from a reluctant deity but words He commands His priests to speak because He intends to bless them. Even the strict rules governing the vow, and the requirement to start over if defiled, show a God who takes devotion seriously while still providing a way to begin again.
basic.crossReferences: Judges 13:5 and 1 Samuel 1:11 describe Samson and Samuel as Nazirites. Ephesians 1:3 says God has blessed believers with every spiritual blessing in Christ. 2 Corinthians 4:6 speaks of the light of the knowledge of God's glory in the face of Christ, echoing the Aaronic blessing's request that God's face shine on His people.
basic.oneStory: God provides a way for ordinary people to consecrate themselves to Him and then, in the same breath, speaks blessing over the whole of His people, grace that does not depend on the vow being kept perfectly. That blessing, God's face shining and giving peace, finds its full and final fulfillment in Jesus Christ, in whom every spiritual blessing is ours.

context.literary:
Numbers 6 falls into two uneven parts. Verses 1 to 21 are the law of the Nazirite, framed as a unit by an opening 'if a man or woman makes a special vow,' verse 2, and a closing 'This is the law of the Nazirite,' verse 21. Inside that frame the law moves in three steps: the three abstentions and what they mean, verses 3 to 8; what happens if the vow is broken by an accidental death, verses 9 to 12; and the ceremony that brings the vow to a close, verses 13 to 20. The key words repeat like a drumbeat. Forms of 'separate' and 'separation' run through almost every verse, and the unit twice declares the Nazirite 'holy,' verses 5 and 8.

Verses 22 to 27 then turn from what one Israelite may offer to God to what God gives all Israel. The blessing is poetry, three lines that each name the LORD and each carry two verbs, and in Hebrew the lines grow longer as they go, three words, then five, then seven. The movement is from the LORD's blessing and keeping, to His shining face and grace, to His lifted countenance and peace. The last verse, verse 27, steps outside the poem to explain it: in speaking these words the priests 'put My name on the Israelites,' and God Himself does the blessing.

The chapter sits between the purity laws of chapter 5 and the dedication gifts of chapter 7. Chapter 5 dealt with what defiles the camp; chapter 6 shows how far holiness can reach, even into the life of a lay man or woman. Placing the blessing here means the long block of instruction given at Sinai, running back through Leviticus and into Exodus, is nearly closed with a benediction before the camp begins to move in chapter 10.
context.historical:
The Nazirite vow was open to 'a man or woman,' verse 2, which is remarkable in a system where priestly holiness belonged to a single family of men. Its requirements come close to those of the high priest. Ordinary priests could defile themselves for close relatives, Leviticus 21:1-3, but the high priest 'must not go near any dead body; he must not defile himself, even for his father or mother,' Leviticus 21:11, the same standard as Numbers 6:6-7. Priests on duty were forbidden wine, Leviticus 10:9. And the Nazirite's hair is called his nezer, verse 7, the word for the 'holy diadem' on the high priest's turban, Exodus 29:6. For the length of the vow an ordinary Israelite carried something of the high priest's holiness in his own body.

The law describes a temporary vow with a set ending. Israel's history also knew lifelong Nazirites dedicated before birth. Samson is 'a Nazirite to God from the womb until the day of his death,' Judges 13:7, and Hannah's vow for Samuel uses the language of the razor that will never come on his head, 1 Samuel 1:11. Amos lists Nazirites alongside prophets as gifts God raised up, and condemns Israel because 'you made the Nazirites drink wine,' Amos 2:11-12. In the New Testament period the vow was still practised: Paul has his head shaved at Cenchrea 'to keep a vow he had made,' Acts 18:18, and in Jerusalem he pays the expenses of four men completing a vow, Acts 21:23-26, which matches the costly offerings of Numbers 6:14-15.

The blessing has a remarkable history of its own. In 1979 two tiny rolled silver amulets were found in a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom, just outside Jerusalem's old city. Usually dated to around the late seventh or early sixth century BC, they carry a form of this blessing and are among the oldest known texts of any passage of Scripture. Israelites were wearing these words on their bodies before the exile.
context.canonical:
Both halves of the chapter echo through the rest of the Bible. The Nazirite reappears in the story of Samson, whose life is a tragic commentary on the vow. He was consecrated from the womb, yet he scoops honey from a lion's carcass, Judges 14:8-9, holds a bridegroom's feast, Judges 14:10, and finally tells Delilah the secret of his hair and loses his strength when the seven braids are shaved, Judges 16:17-19. The vow meant nothing apart from the LORD who stood behind it. Jeremiah uses the Nazirite word when he tells mourning Jerusalem to 'cut off your hair and throw it away,' Jeremiah 7:29, the sign of a consecration forfeited. John the Baptist 'shall never take wine or strong drink,' Luke 1:15, a Nazirite-like life that marks him as a prophet set apart.

The blessing is prayed back to God throughout the Psalms. 'May God be gracious to us and bless us, and cause His face to shine upon us,' Psalm 67:1, turns the blessing into a prayer for the nations, 'that Your ways may be known on earth,' Psalm 67:2. The refrain 'cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved' structures Psalm 80, verses 3, 7 and 19. Psalm 4:6 asks God to 'shine the light of Your face upon us,' Psalm 31:16 prays 'Make Your face shine on Your servant,' and Daniel pleads for God's face to shine 'upon Your desolate sanctuary,' Daniel 9:17. The opposite fear is that God will 'hide My face,' Deuteronomy 31:17, Psalm 13:1.

The New Testament gathers the blessing into Christ. Luke's Gospel opens with a priest, Zechariah, who comes out of the temple 'unable to speak,' Luke 1:22, and so cannot pronounce the blessing over the waiting people, and it closes with Jesus who 'lifted up His hands and blessed them,' Luke 24:50. Paul says the light of God's glory shines 'in the face of Jesus Christ,' 2 Corinthians 4:6. Revelation ends with the blessing's final form: 'They will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads,' Revelation 22:4.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses meant Israel to see that holiness was not only the business of the priests. Any man or woman could step, for a time, into a life marked visibly as 'holy to the LORD,' verse 8. The vow gave ordinary devotion a public shape: people would notice the long hair, the refused cup and the absence at a funeral, and would know that this person had given themselves to God.

He also meant them to learn that holiness is fragile in a world of death. A sudden death in the Nazirite's presence, verse 9, is no one's fault, yet it undoes the vow and requires cleansing, atonement and a fresh start, verse 12. Death and the holiness of God cannot share space, a lesson the whole purity system was teaching.

Most of all, he wanted Israel to hear that the last word over the camp was God's blessing. The priests were not to invent a benediction or to bless in their own name; God gives them the words, verse 23, and the words put His name on the people, verse 27. Israel was to set out from Sinai carrying the name of the LORD, kept, shone upon, pardoned and at peace.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The Nazirite law regulates a voluntary vow. It never commands anyone to take one, but it binds those who do; verse 21 says 'he must fulfill whatever vow he makes,' in line with Numbers 30:2 and Ecclesiastes 5:4-5. Christians are not under the ceremonial law, and the sacrifices that completed the vow have been fulfilled in Christ, so the vow itself is not a pattern for the church.

The principles are another matter. Scripture still honours freely chosen acts of devotion, fasting, abstaining for a season, setting time apart, so long as they are not imposed as law or treated as merit, Colossians 2:20-23. The blessing is different in kind. It is a command to the priests, and the church rightly continues to pronounce it, not as a magic formula but as a declaration of what God has promised to do for those who bear His name in Christ.

debates.question: Does the Nazirite vow have anything to teach Christians today?

views.label: Its form is obsolete
views.case: The vow was bound up with the sanctuary and its sacrifices, verses 13 to 20, and with a purity system that Christ has fulfilled. Believers have no need to prove consecration by abstaining from grapes or leaving their hair uncut, and Paul warns against rules like 'Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch,' Colossians 2:21.

views.label: Its principle of voluntary, visible devotion remains
views.case: Paul himself kept a vow at Cenchrea, Acts 18:18, and helped others complete theirs, Acts 21:23-26, which suggests he saw no conflict between such devotion and the gospel. Freely chosen seasons of consecration, not required but offered, remain a healthy part of Christian life.

debates.bearing: The form belongs to the old covenant, but the impulse is honoured, provided it is voluntary and not a ladder to God's favour. The chapter itself shows that the vow did not make the Nazirite righteous: he still needed a sin offering at its close, verse 14.

debates.question: Does Matthew 2:23, 'He will be called a Nazarene,' refer to the Nazirite vow?

views.label: A reference to Nazareth and the Branch
views.case: Matthew says Jesus lived in Nazareth and so fulfilled what was spoken 'through the prophets,' plural, which suggests a theme rather than one verse. Many connect the name with netzer, the 'Branch' from Jesse's roots, Isaiah 11:1, and with the prophetic theme of a despised, obscure Messiah from an insignificant town.

views.label: An allusion to the Nazirite
views.case: Others hear a play on nazir, since Samson, 'a Nazirite to God from the womb,' was a deliverer set apart before birth, and Matthew loves such patterns. The Greek form of Matthew's word, however, is not the form normally used for the Nazirite.

debates.bearing: The first view is stronger, because Jesus did not live as a Nazirite. He came 'eating and drinking,' Matthew 11:19, and He touched the dead, Mark 5:41. His holiness was not the holiness of separation from defilement but of a presence that removes it. Where the Nazirite theme does surface is at the Last Supper, when He vows not to drink the fruit of the vine until the kingdom, Matthew 26:29.

debates.question: Why does the Nazirite bring a sin offering when the vow is completed without failure, verse 14?

views.label: Purification for leaving a holy state
views.case: The BSB footnote at verse 11 notes that the offering can be called a purification offering. On this view it is not an admission of moral failure but a rite of passage, marking the Nazirite's return from a state of special holiness to ordinary life, much as other purification offerings mark transitions.

views.label: Atonement for unknown failures
views.case: Others read it as a humble acknowledgment that even a vow kept outwardly was kept by a sinner, and that any unnoticed lapses during the period need covering before God.

debates.bearing: Both readings guard against pride. Whatever the Nazirite achieved, he ended at the altar with the same offerings as everyone else, his empty hands filled by the priest only so that he could present to God what belonged to God, verses 19 and 20.

study.originalLanguages:
The vow is introduced with an unusual verb. The man or woman who 'makes a special vow,' verse 2, uses a form of pala, the root of wonder and the extraordinary, the word used for God's wonders in the exodus. The same expression appears in Leviticus 27:2 for special vows involving persons. A Nazirite vow is not routine; it is something out of the ordinary, a wonder of devotion.

The title itself, nazir, comes from nazar, to separate or dedicate, and the BSB footnote gives both senses, 'one separated or one consecrated.' Separation is from something, the vine, the razor and the dead, but it is always for someone, 'to the LORD,' verses 2, 5, 6 and 8. The same root gives nezer, crown or diadem, and verse 7 calls the uncut hair 'the crown of consecration to his God.' Elsewhere nezer is the 'holy diadem' of the high priest, Exodus 29:6 and 39:30, and the royal crown taken from Saul, 2 Samuel 1:10, and put on young Joash, 2 Kings 11:12. Joseph is called 'the prince of his brothers,' Genesis 49:26 and Deuteronomy 33:16, using nazir, the one set apart among them. The Nazirite's hair was a crown he grew rather than wore. Jeremiah uses nezer for Jerusalem's hair when he tells her to cut it off in mourning, Jeremiah 7:29.

The ban on the vine is total. Verse 4 forbids 'anything that comes from the grapevine,' literally 'the vine of wine,' and closes with two rare words for the smallest parts of the grape, rendered 'seeds or skins.' Their exact meaning was already uncertain to ancient translators, but the point is clear: not even the least part of the fruit.

When the vow is broken by a death, verse 12 says 'the preceding days shall not be counted,' literally 'the former days shall fall.' They drop away as though they had never been. The Nazirite must also bring a sin offering because 'he has sinned by being in the presence of the dead body,' verse 11. The verb chata here names not a moral fault but a state that must be purged, which is why the BSB footnote allows 'purification offering.'

The blessing turns on four pairs of verbs. The first, barak and shamar, 'bless' and 'keep,' combine gift and protection; shamar is the verb of Psalm 121, 'The LORD will guard you from all evil,' Psalm 121:7. The second, 'cause His face to shine,' ya'er panav, uses the causative of the verb or, to be light, the root of the light God called into being in Genesis 1:3, and pairs it with chanan, 'be gracious,' the undeserved favour of Exodus 33:19. The third, 'lift up His countenance,' nasa panim, is an idiom for looking on someone with favour. When Cain's 'countenance fell,' Genesis 4:5-6, it was the opposite motion. Jacob hoped Esau would 'accept me,' literally lift up my face, Genesis 32:20, and Malachi asks whether God will 'show you favor,' Malachi 1:9, with the same idiom. Psalm 4:6 fuses the second and third lines into one prayer.

The last word of the poem is shalom, peace, which in Hebrew is not only the absence of conflict but wholeness, soundness and well-being in every direction. The poem ends on the note of a life made whole before God.

Finally, verse 27 uses sum, to put or set, for placing the name on Israel. It is the language Deuteronomy uses for the place God chooses 'to establish as a dwelling for His Name,' Deuteronomy 12:5. What God does for the sanctuary, He does for the people: they carry His name, as Deuteronomy 28:10 says, 'called by the name of the LORD.'

typology.type: The Nazirite, a life wholly set apart to God, Numbers 6:2-8
typology.fulfillment: The Nazirite was holy for a season by abstaining from what defiled. Christ is 'holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners,' Hebrews 7:26, and says, 'For them I sanctify Myself,' John 17:19. The escalation is that His holiness does not depend on distance from uncleanness. He eats with sinners and touches the dead without defilement, because His holiness overcomes theirs. The type also breaks at a telling point: the Nazirite's consecration could be lost in an instant by a sudden death, verse 9, but Christ entered death itself and was not defiled, rising on the third day.

typology.type: The priest pronouncing the blessing with lifted hands, Numbers 6:23-27 and Leviticus 9:22
typology.fulfillment: Aaron 'lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them,' Leviticus 9:22, and his sons were commanded to speak the words of Numbers 6. At the close of Luke's Gospel Jesus leads His disciples out to Bethany, 'lifted up His hands and blessed them,' and while blessing them is carried into heaven, Luke 24:50-51. His last earthly act is the priestly benediction, and He goes on blessing from the heavenly sanctuary, where He always lives to intercede, Hebrews 7:25. The type falls short because Aaron's sons could speak the blessing but not secure it; Christ both speaks it and is its substance.

typology.type: The LORD's face shining on His people, Numbers 6:25
typology.fulfillment: Israel prayed for God's face to shine on them, yet no one could see His face and live. Moses' face only reflected the glory after speaking with God, Exodus 34:29-30. In Christ the prayer is answered: God 'made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ,' 2 Corinthians 4:6, and 'the one and only Son' has made Him known, John 1:18. The fulfilment is still partial, for the full vision awaits the day when 'They will see His face,' Revelation 22:4.

typology.type: The peace that crowns the blessing, Numbers 6:26
typology.fulfillment: The priestly blessing ends in shalom, wholeness under God's favour. The angels announce at Jesus' birth 'on earth peace to men on whom His favor rests,' Luke 2:14, the lifted countenance and the peace joined together. Paul says that, being justified through faith, 'we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,' Romans 5:1, and that 'He Himself is our peace,' Ephesians 2:14. What Israel received as a spoken promise, the church receives as a person, though its full extent, the end of all conflict, still awaits the new creation.

study.christ:
The chapter points to Christ first through the Nazirite, though by contrast as much as correspondence. The Nazirite was holy by withdrawal: no wine, no razor, no contact with the dead. Jesus was not a Nazirite. He came 'eating and drinking,' Matthew 11:19, and He took a dead girl by the hand, Mark 5:41. Yet Hebrews calls Him 'holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners,' Hebrews 7:26. His holiness runs in the opposite direction to the Nazirite's. Where the Nazirite had to be protected from death, death could not hold Christ; where a sudden death undid the Nazirite's vow, Christ's death completed His.

There is one moment when Jesus does take a Nazirite-like vow. At the Last Supper He says, 'I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I drink it anew with you in My Father's kingdom,' Matthew 26:29. He sets Himself apart for the work of the cross, and John records Him praying, 'For them I sanctify Myself, so that they too may be sanctified,' John 17:19. His consecration is not for His own sake but for His people.

The blessing points to Christ more directly still. Each line of it finds its answer in Him. 'Bless you and keep you': Paul says God 'has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing,' Ephesians 1:3, and Jesus says of those the Father gave Him, 'I protected and preserved them by Your name,' John 17:12. 'Cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious': the glory of God shines 'in the face of Jesus Christ,' 2 Corinthians 4:6, and 'the Word became flesh,' John 1:14, 'full of grace and truth.' 'Lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace': 'we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,' Romans 5:1, and Jesus says, 'My peace I give to you,' John 14:27.

Luke frames his whole Gospel with the blessing. It begins with Zechariah the priest serving in the temple, and when he comes out to the people he is 'unable to speak to them,' Luke 1:22. The blessing the people waited for could not be spoken. It ends with Jesus lifting up His hands and blessing His disciples as He is carried into heaven, Luke 24:50-51. The Great High Priest completes what the priest of the old covenant could not.

The name that the priests placed on Israel, verse 27, is finally placed on the redeemed in the presence of the Lamb: 'His name will be on their foreheads,' Revelation 22:4. Some in the church have heard the threefold 'LORD' of the blessing as a hint of the Trinity, and Paul's closing blessing in 2 Corinthians 13:14 is itself threefold. The text of Numbers does not teach that directly, and it is wiser to say that the one God who blesses here is revealed in the New Testament as Father, Son and Spirit, than to claim Moses saw it.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows about God is that He welcomes devotion from anyone. The vow is open to 'a man or woman,' verse 2, of any tribe, and it lets an ordinary Israelite share a level of holiness otherwise reserved for the high priest. God does not keep holiness locked inside one family. He invites the whole people to be 'holy to the LORD,' verse 8, which anticipates the call of 1 Peter 1:15-16, 'Be holy, because I am holy.'

He takes holiness seriously. Death in the Nazirite's presence, even sudden and innocent, verse 9, breaks the consecration and demands atonement and a fresh beginning. That is not harshness but a lesson: the living God and death are opposites, and anything consecrated to Him must be kept from death's touch. Yet the law provides a way back the very next week, verses 10 to 12. God does not cast off the one whose vow was broken; He restarts it.

He is the source of all blessing. The priests speak, but God says, 'I will bless them,' verse 27. The blessing is not something Israel extracts or the priests manufacture. It flows from God's own will to do good, and its six verbs describe what He does: He blesses, keeps, makes His face shine, is gracious, lifts His countenance and gives peace. Every verb has the LORD as its subject.

He is a God with a face. The blessing uses the most personal language possible: God turning toward His people, His face lit with favour. It is the opposite of the dreaded hidden face of Deuteronomy 31:17 and Psalm 13:1. The God of Israel is not an impersonal force but a person who looks on His people with pleasure.

He is gracious. The verb of the second line is the one God uses of Himself when He proclaims His name to Moses, 'I will have mercy on whom I have mercy,' Exodus 33:19. The grace comes before and beneath every command. That is why the blessing follows the laws of chapters 5 and 6 and not the other way around.

He gives His name. To have God's name placed on a people, verse 27, is to belong to Him, to be under His protection and to represent Him before the world, Deuteronomy 28:10. It is a costly gift, because it binds God's reputation to His people's life.

For worship, the chapter invites two responses. One is glad devotion, offering God freely what He has not required, as a thank offering from a grateful heart. The other is to receive. Every time the church hears the blessing spoken, it is being told what God intends to do: to keep, to shine, to be gracious and to give peace.

crossReferences.note: The rules for the high priest, who must not go near a dead body or defile himself even for his father or mother because the consecration of the anointing oil is on him. The Nazirite of Numbers 6:6-7 keeps the same standard, a lay person sharing the high priest's degree of holiness.

The 'holy diadem' attached to Aaron's turban is the nezer, the same word Numbers 6:7 uses for the Nazirite's uncut hair, 'the crown of consecration to his God.' The Nazirite's hair was his diadem, a sign that his head belonged to the LORD.

The angel tells Samson's mother to avoid wine and unclean food, and that no razor shall come on her son's head, because he will be 'a Nazirite to God from the womb.' It shows a lifelong form of the vow imposed by God rather than chosen, and it sets up Samson's tragic misuse of his consecration.

God counts the Nazirites among His gifts to Israel alongside the prophets, and indicts the people for making the Nazirites drink wine. Pressuring the consecrated to break faith was treated as an attack on God's own work among them.

Paul, at the elders' request, purifies himself with four men under a vow and pays their expenses so they can have their heads shaved. The vow of Numbers 6, with its costly closing offerings, was still being kept in Jerusalem, and Paul honoured it.

The psalm prays the priestly blessing back to God, asking Him to be gracious, bless and cause His face to shine, and then widens it: 'that Your ways may be known on earth, Your salvation among all nations.' The blessing of Israel was meant to overflow to the world.

The refrain of the psalm, 'Restore us, O God, and cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved,' takes the words of Numbers 6:25 into a time of national ruin. The shining face becomes the hope of rescue when blessing seems withdrawn.

Jesus leads His disciples to Bethany, lifts up His hands and blesses them, and is carried into heaven while blessing them. The priestly gesture of Leviticus 9:22 and Numbers 6 becomes the last act of the risen Christ on earth.

The God who said 'Let light shine out of darkness' has shone in believers' hearts with the light of His glory 'in the face of Jesus Christ.' The prayer that the LORD's face would shine on His people is answered in the face of the Son.

Justified through faith, believers have peace with God through Jesus Christ. The shalom that closes the Aaronic blessing is grounded here in the verdict of justification, not in the worshipper's success in keeping vows.

In the new creation God's servants 'will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads.' Both halves of the blessing's promise, the shining face of Numbers 6:25 and the name placed on the people in 6:27, reach their final form.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with blessing. God blessed the living creatures and then blessed the man and woman, Genesis 1:28, and the first sin brought curse instead. God's call of Abraham reversed the direction: 'I will bless you,' and 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:2-3. The priestly blessing of Numbers 6 is that promise given liturgical form. The descendants of Abraham, now a nation camped at Sinai, are to hear God's blessing spoken over them day by day, and to carry His name.

The Nazirite law belongs to the same story from the other side. Humanity was made to belong to God, but sin and death broke that consecration. The Nazirite shows, in one person's body for a season, what a life wholly given to God looks like, and how easily death can spoil it. Israel's later history shows the pattern writ large: Samson squanders his consecration, the people make the Nazirites drink wine, Amos 2:12, and the nation that bore God's name profanes it until God hides His face in exile, Deuteronomy 31:17.

Yet the blessing is not withdrawn. Psalm 80 prays through the ruin for God's face to shine again, and the prophets promise a day when it will. In Christ it does. The truly consecrated one, holy and undefiled, enters death and is not defiled but defeats it. The face of God shines in His face, 2 Corinthians 4:6, and He gives His people peace, Romans 5:1. Through Him 'the blessing promised to Abraham' comes to the Gentiles, Galatians 3:14, so that the prayer of Psalm 67 for the nations is answered.

The story ends where the blessing was heading. In the new creation there is no more curse, and God's servants 'will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads,' Revelation 22:3-4. The people the priests blessed with words will live forever in the full light of the face they prayed would shine on them, kept, shown grace and at peace.

sermon.title: Benediction
sermon.why: Preached on Numbers 6:22-27 as part of a series on the elements of corporate worship, Keller unpacks the Aaronic blessing line by line, showing how God's blessing, grace, and peace are ultimately given to His people through Christ.

quiz.q: What were the main restrictions of the Nazirite vow described in this chapter?

options.text: Abstaining from wine and anything from the grapevine, not cutting the hair, and not going near a dead body.
options.note: Verses 3 to 6 list these three restrictions exactly.

options.text: Fasting from all food for the entire length of the vow.
options.note: No general fast is described; the restrictions are specific to wine, hair, and the dead.

options.text: Living permanently outside the camp.
options.note: Nazirites remained within the community; no requirement to leave the camp is given.

options.text: No specific restrictions are mentioned.
options.note: Verses 3 to 6 detail the restrictions clearly.

quiz.q: What had to happen if a Nazirite was suddenly defiled by a death nearby?

options.text: They shaved their head on the seventh day, offered specific sacrifices, and started the days of separation over again.
options.note: Verses 9 to 12 describe this exact process.

options.text: The vow was permanently cancelled with no remedy.
options.note: A remedy and a restart process are given, not a permanent cancellation.

options.text: Nothing; accidental defilement did not affect the vow.
options.note: This contradicts the explicit instructions in verses 9 to 12.

options.text: The text gives no instructions for this situation.
options.note: Verses 9 to 12 address it directly.

quiz.q: What offerings did a Nazirite bring when the vow was completed?

options.text: A burnt offering, a sin offering, a peace offering, along with grain and drink offerings and a basket of unleavened bread.
options.note: Verses 13 to 15 list these offerings in full.

options.text: Only a single lamb, with nothing else required.
options.note: This understates the fuller set of offerings actually required.

options.text: A monetary payment to the priest instead of any sacrifice.
options.note: The text specifies animal and grain offerings, not a monetary substitute.

options.text: No offerings are mentioned at the completion of the vow.
options.note: Verses 13 to 15 detail the required offerings.

quiz.q: What is the central request of the Aaronic blessing in verses 24 to 26?

options.text: That the LORD bless and keep His people, cause His face to shine on them and be gracious, and lift up His countenance and give them peace.
options.note: This is the blessing's content exactly, in three rising lines.

options.text: That the LORD grant Israel military victory over their enemies.
options.note: Military victory is not the content of this particular blessing.

options.text: That the LORD provide abundant harvests every year.
options.note: Harvests are not mentioned in this blessing.

options.text: The blessing's content is not described.
options.note: Verses 24 to 26 give the blessing's exact wording.

quiz.q: According to verse 27, what is the effect of the priests pronouncing this blessing?

options.text: The LORD puts His own name on the Israelites, and He Himself blesses them.
options.note: Verse 27 states this directly.

options.text: The blessing has only symbolic value with no real effect.
options.note: Verse 27 explicitly states that God Himself blesses as a result.

options.text: The blessing applies only to the priests who speak it.
options.note: The blessing is spoken over the Israelites, not reserved for the priests alone.

options.text: No effect of the blessing is stated.
options.note: Verse 27 states the effect explicitly.

questions: The Nazirite vow was a voluntary way to mark a season of special devotion to God. What would it look like for you to intentionally set apart a season, or even a daily habit, as a visible act of devotion to the Lord?

A single accidental defilement meant the Nazirite's count of days started over completely. Where have you let a single failure convince you that you must abandon a commitment entirely, rather than simply beginning again?

The Aaronic blessing is not a wish but words God commands to be spoken, promising He will actually bless, keep, and give peace to His people. Do you receive God's blessing as something He delights to give, or as something you must earn?

God asks that His face shine upon His people, and that request is answered fully in Jesus, in whom we see the glory of God. Where do you need to remember this week that in Christ, God's face is turned toward you in favor, not judgment?
This blessing closes with God placing His own name on His people. How does knowing you are called by God's name, His own possession, change how you see your identity today?

translationNotes.note: The vow of a Nazirite renders nazir, from a root meaning to separate or consecrate; the term describes the status of the person, not merely the vow itself.
The three-part blessing rises in length and fullness with each line in the Hebrew, a deliberate poetic crescendo often less audible in translation but clear when read aloud in the original.
They shall put My name on the Israelites uses covenant language elsewhere associated with ownership and belonging, so the blessing is inseparable from God claiming His people as His own.
